claim: Well-cooked egg is safer than raw or lightly cooked egg for first introduction
stakes_rationale: Cooking egg thoroughly costs nothing; raw-egg first exposures risk reactions from hives to rare anaphylaxis, so severity is contested.

claim: Introducing peanut before 6 months of age reduces the risk of peanut allergy
draft_exposure: Introducing peanut before 6 months of age
stakes_rationale: Regular peanut exposure takes deliberate effort; a missed prevention window can mean lifelong anaphylaxis-capable allergy, though many would rate that manageable.
guidance_note: The AAP recommends peanut as early as 4 to 6 months for high-risk babies, while the NHS says around 6 months for all babies and does not recommend solids before then; both pages are current post-LEAP guidance, and neither says introducing peanut before 6 months benefits low-risk babies.
nhs_says: Introduce peanut from around 6 months, when you start solids. Delaying it past 6 to 12 months may raise your baby's chance of peanut allergy.
aap_says: Babies at high risk of peanut allergy (severe eczema or egg allergy) should try peanut foods as early as 4 to 6 months, after other solids.

claim: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months gives the best health outcomes
stakes_rationale: Six months exclusive demands body, sleep and career, and supply is not fully controllable; averted harms are mostly recoverable infections in rich countries.

claim: Bed-sharing increases the risk of sudden unexpected infant death
stakes_rationale: Avoiding bed-sharing is easy with some babies and a nightly battle with contact-sleepers; the risk side is infant death.
guidance_note: The AAP tells parents not to bed-share at all and to room-share on a separate surface, whereas the NHS accepts that some parents will bed-share and gives conditions for doing it more safely alongside a list of circumstances in which it is never safe.
nhs_says: A separate cot in your room is safest, but if you do share a bed, do it safely. Never co-sleep after alcohol, drugs, smoking, or if very tired.
aap_says: Do not share a bed with your baby. Sleep in the same room but on separate surfaces; room-sharing without bed-sharing protects against SIDS.

claim: Behavioural sleep training causes lasting harm to infant attachment or stress regulation
draft_outcome: lasting harm to infant attachment or stress regulation
stakes_rationale: Acting means living with prolonged night waking; if training truly damaged attachment that is lasting harm, but the severity is hotly contested.
guidance_note: The AAP actively advises giving a baby time to resettle without rushing in, while the NHS warns that a baby left to 'cry it out' may still be distressed and urges responding to cries; neither page states a position on the claim's specific question of lasting harm to attachment or stress regulation.
nhs_says: Respond to your baby's cries. A baby left to cry it out may go quiet but can still be distressed when no one comes.
aap_says: Put your baby down drowsy and give them a chance to resettle themselves rather than rushing in. Learning to self-soothe is a normal skill.

claim: Rice-based infant foods contain concerning levels of inorganic arsenic
stakes_rationale: Diversifying away from cheap rice staples is doable; chronic arsenic's neurodevelopmental effect is real but its size is contested.

claim: Teaching baby sign language accelerates spoken language development
stakes_rationale: Classes and consistent signing take effort; spoken-language acceleration largely fails to replicate.

claim: Print books produce richer parent-child interaction than electronic books
stakes_rationale: Choosing print over a tablet costs nothing; the interaction difference is subtle either way.

claim: Plant-based milks are nutritionally inadequate as a main drink for infants
stakes_rationale: Formula costs more than oat milk; plant milks as a main drink have caused documented severe protein-energy malnutrition.

claim: Crawling is not a required precursor to walking
stakes_rationale: A reassurance claim; the only cost of disbelief is needless worry and perhaps unneeded therapy referrals.

claim: Iron-rich complementary foods are needed from 6 months
stakes_rationale: Iron-rich foods take planning and money; iron deficiency affects development but is detectable and treatable.

claim: Fewer toys in the environment leads to higher quality play
stakes_rationale: Buying fewer toys saves money; play-quality differences are subtle and short-term.

claim: Swaddling becomes unsafe once an infant can roll over
stakes_rationale: Stopping swaddling at rolling costs a few unsettled nights; a swaddled baby who rolls risks suffocation.

claim: Infants learn less from video than from equivalent live interaction
stakes_rationale: Preferring live interaction costs nothing; the foregone difference is a learning-efficiency gap, not a lasting deficit.

claim: Infants who can self-settle at bedtime wake less during the night
stakes_rationale: Teaching self-settling overlaps with sleep training in effort; the foregone benefit is fewer night wakings.

claim: Most infants sleep through the night by 6 months of age
stakes_rationale: Descriptive rather than actionable; it is unclear what a parent does with it, so the stakes framing barely applies.

claim: Baby-led weaning increases the risk of choking
stakes_rationale: Choosing safer textures is free; a true choking risk is potentially fatal, but most reported events are harmless gagging.

claim: Hydrolysed formula prevents allergic disease in high-risk infants
stakes_rationale: Hydrolysed formula costs several times standard formula for months; the averted harm is eczema and allergy, and affordability varies hugely.

claim: Delaying peanut introduction beyond 12 months increases the risk of peanut allergy
stakes_rationale: Introducing peanut by 12 months is cheap and simple; the harm side is the same lifelong anaphylaxis-capable allergy.

claim: Honey should be avoided before 12 months because of infant botulism risk
tested_as: Honey consumption before 12 months is associated with infant botulism
stakes_rationale: Not giving honey costs literally nothing; infant botulism can paralyse and kill.
nhs_says: Do not give honey until your child is over 1 year old. Honey can contain bacteria that cause infant botulism, a very serious illness.
aap_says: Do not give honey to a baby under 12 months. Honey carries botulism spores. It is safe from age 1 onwards.

claim: Ultra-processed foods in infancy are associated with poorer diet quality
stakes_rationale: Avoiding ultra-processed food means sustained scratch cooking a stretched parent may not manage; poorer diet quality is a weak, indirect harm.

claim: Cow's milk should not be given as a main drink before 12 months
tested_as: Cow's milk as the main drink before 12 months is associated with worse outcomes such as iron deficiency
draft_exposure: Cow's milk as the main drink before 12 months is
draft_outcome: worse outcomes such as iron deficiency
stakes_rationale: Formula to 12 months costs real money that cow's milk would save; the averted harm is treatable iron-deficiency anaemia.
nhs_says: Do not give cow's milk as your baby's main drink until 12 months. It does not have the right balance of nutrients for them before then.
aap_says: Do not give cow's milk before about 12 months. It can irritate the gut, cause blood loss and lead to iron-deficiency anaemia.

claim: Baby walkers increase the risk of injury
stakes_rationale: Not buying a walker saves money; walker injuries include stair falls and skull fractures.

claim: Breastfed infants require vitamin D supplementation
stakes_rationale: Drops are cheap but need a daily habit; missed supplementation risks rickets, which is treatable when caught.
nhs_says: Give breastfed babies a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms from birth to age 1. Formula-fed babies on 500ml a day do not need one.
aap_says: Give breastfed and partly breastfed babies 400 IU of vitamin D a day, starting in the first few days of life.

claim: Vitamin K at birth prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn
stakes_rationale: A routine injection offered at birth; declining risks haemorrhagic disease, including fatal intracranial bleeding.
nhs_says: Your baby will be offered a vitamin K injection after birth. It prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, a rare bleeding disorder.
aap_says: Every newborn should get a vitamin K shot at birth. One injection protects your baby from vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

claim: High-quality group childcare improves cognitive outcomes
stakes_rationale: High-quality childcare is expensive, scarce, and often simply unavailable; quality effects on cognition are real but modest and setting-dependent.

claim: Placing infants on their back to sleep reduces the risk of SIDS
draft_exposure: Placing infants on their back to sleep
stakes_rationale: Sleep position is free; the averted outcome is SIDS.
nhs_says: Always put your baby down to sleep on their back, feet at the end of the cot. This is listed as a way to reduce the risk of SIDS.
aap_says: Put your baby on their back for every nap and every night until age 1. Back sleepers are far less likely to die suddenly.

claim: Overheating during sleep increases the risk of SIDS
stakes_rationale: Dressing the baby lighter costs nothing; overheating is a SIDS risk factor, so the harm end is death.

claim: Pacifier use at sleep onset reduces the risk of SIDS
stakes_rationale: Pacifiers are cheap, though some babies refuse and weaning comes later; the outcome on the table is SIDS.

claim: Room-sharing without bed-sharing reduces the risk of SIDS
stakes_rationale: Keeping the cot in the parents' room costs space and some adult sleep; the averted outcome is SIDS.

claim: Soft bedding and pillows in the sleep space increase the risk of SIDS
draft_exposure: Soft bedding and pillows in the sleep space
stakes_rationale: An empty cot is cheaper than a decorated one; soft-bedding deaths are suffocation deaths.

claim: Behavioural sleep interventions improve infant sleep and maternal wellbeing
stakes_rationale: A bounded but emotionally taxing protocol some parents find unbearable; forgoing it can mean months of family sleep loss.

claim: Frequent night waking is developmentally normal in the first year
stakes_rationale: A reassurance claim: accepting normal waking costs nothing, and disbelieving it mainly costs worry.

claim: Infants aged 4-12 months need 12-16 hours of sleep per 24 hours
stakes_rationale: Providing sleep opportunity is free and sleep cannot be forced; individual need varies too widely for the range to bite.

claim: Infant massage supports growth and development
stakes_rationale: A few pleasant minutes at most; growth effects outside preterm populations are negligible.

claim: Infant swimming programmes improve motor skill development
stakes_rationale: Classes cost money and pool trips; motor benefits over ordinary play are small.

claim: More outdoor time in early childhood reduces the risk of myopia
draft_exposure: More outdoor time in early childhood
stakes_rationale: Daily outdoor time demands parent hours and weather tolerance; myopia is lifelong and progressive, though correctable.

claim: Infants should have at least 30 minutes of tummy time or active play daily
tested_as: Greater daily tummy time or active play in infancy is associated with better motor development
draft_exposure: Greater daily tummy time or active play in infancy is
stakes_rationale: Thirty daily active minutes takes scheduling; below-target babies still mostly hit milestones on time.

claim: Prolonged sedentary or restrained time is associated with poorer development
draft_exposure: Prolonged sedentary or restrained time is
stakes_rationale: Car seats and strollers are how life gets done; reducing restraint takes effort against a small developmental effect.

claim: Introducing multiple allergenic foods early reduces overall food allergy risk
stakes_rationale: Keeping several allergens in regular rotation is sustained effort trial families struggled with; the payoff is fewer manageable food allergies.

claim: Introducing egg between 4 and 6 months reduces the risk of egg allergy
stakes_rationale: Cooked egg is cheap to offer; egg allergy is usually outgrown, so the missed prevention is recoverable.

claim: Added salt should be avoided in the infant diet
tested_as: Higher sodium intake in infancy is associated with worse health outcomes
draft_exposure: Higher sodium intake in infancy is
stakes_rationale: Not salting baby's food costs nothing; sodium loads strain immature kidneys and shape taste, though everyday exposures are modest.

claim: Free sugars should be avoided before 24 months
tested_as: Free sugar intake before 24 months is associated with worse health outcomes
draft_exposure: Free sugar intake before 24 months is
stakes_rationale: Avoiding all free sugars to 24 months means fighting the entire food environment; the averted harms are caries and weight gain.

claim: Bilingual exposure in infancy does not delay language development
draft_exposure: Bilingual exposure in infancy does not
stakes_rationale: Continuing the home language costs nothing; abandoning it out of misplaced fear sacrifices a language and family connection.

claim: Conversational turn-taking predicts language outcomes better than word count alone
draft_outcome: language outcomes better than word count alone
stakes_rationale: Responding to babble costs nothing; this is a claim about which metric predicts best, not a new behaviour.

claim: Reading aloud to infants improves later language development
stakes_rationale: Daily reading needs books and a routine, though libraries are free; the foregone benefit is language development.

claim: Shared reading beginning in infancy improves later literacy outcomes
stakes_rationale: Same daily habit as reading aloud; literacy gaps that start in infancy are real but remediable.

claim: The amount of adult speech directed at an infant predicts vocabulary growth
draft_exposure: The amount of adult speech directed at an infant
stakes_rationale: Narrating your day to a baby is free; sparse language input measurably slows vocabulary growth.

claim: Early cow's milk introduction increases the risk of iron deficiency anaemia
stakes_rationale: Same action as the main-drink rule: pay for formula longer to avoid treatable iron-deficiency anaemia.

claim: Fruit juice should be avoided before 12 months
tested_as: Fruit juice consumption before 12 months is associated with worse health outcomes
draft_exposure: Fruit juice consumption before 12 months is
stakes_rationale: Skipping juice saves money; the averted harms are dental caries and displaced nutrition, real but reversible.

claim: Barefoot walking supports healthy foot development in early childhood
draft_outcome: healthy foot development in early childhood
stakes_rationale: Skipping shoes indoors saves money; foot-development differences are small and self-correcting.

claim: Prolonged time in walkers or containers delays motor development
draft_exposure: Prolonged time in walkers or containers
stakes_rationale: Limiting prolonged container time costs little; the harm is a transient motor delay that catches up.

claim: Tummy time supports gross motor development
stakes_rationale: Scheduling tummy time with a protesting baby is effort; motor milestones converge regardless within normal ranges.

claim: Tummy time reduces positional plagiocephaly
stakes_rationale: Same scheduling effort as tummy time; skipping it risks flat-head severe enough for distressing, expensive helmet therapy.

claim: Omega-3 DHA intake in infancy supports brain and visual development
stakes_rationale: Fish or supplements cost something; trial effects on cognition and vision are small and inconsistent.

claim: Early formal academic instruction improves later school achievement
stakes_rationale: Formal instruction costs money and toddler goodwill; achievement advantages fade out within a few school years.

claim: Unstructured play supports cognitive and social development
stakes_rationale: Unstructured play is the cheapest activity there is; children find play regardless, so marginal deprivation effects are small.

claim: Musical activity in infancy supports language and auditory development
stakes_rationale: Singing to a baby is free; auditory-development advantages are small laboratory effects.

claim: Pretend play supports social cognition and theory of mind
draft_outcome: social cognition and theory of mind
stakes_rationale: Pretend play emerges by itself; theory-of-mind effects are correlational and small.

claim: Educational apps improve learning outcomes in toddlers
stakes_rationale: Apps cost money and screen-time trade-offs; skipping them forgoes learning gains that barely replicate.

claim: Early screen exposure is associated with later attention problems
stakes_rationale: Limiting early screens takes ongoing willpower; attention problems are a real but manageable harm.

claim: Screen use during meals is associated with poorer eating behaviour
stakes_rationale: No screens at the table costs nothing but habit; distracted eating undermines responsive feeding and satiety cues.

claim: Higher screen time in infancy is associated with language delay
draft_exposure: Higher screen time in infancy is associated with language
stakes_rationale: Cutting screen time removes a convenient pacifier for busy days; language delay is real but responds to intervention.

claim: Higher screen time is associated with higher BMI in early childhood
stakes_rationale: Screen limits take sustained enforcement; the BMI association is small against an outcome dominated by diet and genetics.

claim: Higher screen time is associated with shorter sleep in young children
stakes_rationale: Enforcing screen limits is a daily negotiation; the harm side is shorter sleep, which affects everything else.

claim: Background television reduces the quantity and quality of parent-child interaction
draft_outcome: the quantity and quality of parent-child interaction
stakes_rationale: Switching the TV off costs nothing; background TV measurably suppresses the parent-child talk that drives language.

claim: Adult co-viewing reduces the negative effects of screen time
draft_outcome: the negative effects of screen time
stakes_rationale: Co-viewing demands parent time precisely when screens are used to buy time; the moderating benefit is small.

claim: Screen media should be avoided before 18-24 months
tested_as: Screen media exposure before 18-24 months is associated with worse developmental outcomes
draft_exposure: Screen media exposure before 18-24 months is
stakes_rationale: Total screen avoidance removes a stretched parent's only break; the harms are language and developmental delays, real but recoverable.
nhs_says: Avoid screens for babies and toddlers. If you do use one, watch together and talk about it so it becomes a shared, interactive activity.
aap_says: Avoid TV and apps before 18 months, apart from video chat with family. Babies learn from real interaction, not from screens.

claim: Video chatting is an acceptable exception to infant screen-time limits
tested_as: Video chatting with a live partner is associated with better outcomes than pre-recorded screen content in infancy
draft_exposure: Video chatting with a live partner is
draft_outcome: better outcomes than pre-recorded screen content in infancy
stakes_rationale: Allowing video calls is a permission, not an effort; banning them merely forgoes some family connection.

claim: A consistent bedtime routine improves infant sleep
stakes_rationale: A consistent routine takes discipline every evening; the cost of skipping it is measurably poorer sleep for everyone.

claim: Screen exposure before bedtime worsens infant sleep
stakes_rationale: Moving screens away from bedtime costs nothing; the harm side is poorer sleep, which compounds for the whole household.

claim: Daytime naps support memory consolidation and learning in infants
draft_outcome: memory consolidation and learning in infants
stakes_rationale: Babies nap anyway; the missed memory-consolidation benefits are laboratory-scale, not milestones.

claim: Short sleep duration in infancy is associated with later obesity
draft_exposure: Short sleep duration in infancy is
stakes_rationale: Protecting sleep takes routine effort; the obesity link is one small influence on an outcome with many larger causes.

claim: Baby-led weaning supports healthy appetite self-regulation
stakes_rationale: A feeding style, not an expense; appetite self-regulation differences are small on an outcome that varies widely anyway.

claim: Repeated exposure increases an infant's acceptance of vegetables
stakes_rationale: Repeatedly offering rejected vegetables wastes food and patience; the downside is only pickier eating within normal variation.

claim: Delaying lumpy textures beyond 9 months increases later feeding difficulties
stakes_rationale: Offering lumps by 9 months costs nothing; missing the window means feeding difficulties that are real but treatable.

claim: Complementary feeding should begin at around 6 months of age
tested_as: Introducing complementary foods at around 6 months is associated with better outcomes than introducing them earlier or later
draft_exposure: Introducing complementary foods at around 6 months is
draft_outcome: better outcomes than introducing them earlier or later
stakes_rationale: Timing solids near 6 months costs nothing; late starts risk iron deficiency, early starts carry modest infection risk.
nhs_says: Start solid foods when your baby is around 6 months old. Before that, breast milk or first infant formula gives them everything they need.
aap_says: Give only breast milk for about the first 6 months, then start solid foods once your baby shows they are developmentally ready.

claim: Introducing solid foods before 4 months increases health risks
stakes_rationale: Waiting until 4 months costs nothing; very early solids carry infection, choking and obesity risks that are real but recoverable.
